questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why industry came first to Britain
questions.learningObjective: explain the interaction of cheap fuel and high wages in British industrial take-off
questions.stem: In the 1750s manufacturers in several European states all had merchants, colonies, and coal within reach. What combination of conditions let output per worker rise first in Britain?

options.text: Cheap coal and high wages rewarded machines and fuel power

options.misconception: reverses both the wage and the fuel incentive
options.text: Cheap coal and low wages discouraged labor-saving machines

options.misconception: describes conditions that punish capital investment
options.text: High wages and cheap coal punished firms that invested

options.misconception: claims hand work was cheapest where fuel was cheap
options.text: Low wages and cheap coal made hand work the cheapest option

questions.explanation: When fuel was cheap and labor dear, machines that saved hands or burned coal became the profitable choice, so Britain's high wages and accessible coal reinforced each other. The tempting answer reverses both variables and describes the country in which machines were a luxury a firm could decline.
questions.hint: Which of the two prices made machinery pay for itself?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why gathering work under one roof beat scattered cottage production
questions.stem: In the 1780s a merchant found that handloom weavers in scattered cottages missed delivery dates whenever yarn ran short. What advantage did a mill owner see in gathering them under one roof?

options.text: One supervisor could police hours and replace a missing hand

options.misconception: confuses wages with the older system of paying in goods
options.text: Rural weavers could be paid in goods rather than in money

options.misconception: invents a rule letting children run looms untrained
options.text: Cottage looms could be worked by children without training

options.misconception: reverses the effect of centralized inspection on quality
options.text: Central workshops allowed poorer yarn without any inspection

questions.explanation: The scattered system lost orders precisely because nobody controlled timing or skill, so machines and workers in one place made the pace visible and every hand interchangeable. The tempting answer is about paying in goods, which describes the older cottage pay rather than any advantage of location.
questions.hint: What went wrong when yarn ran out in a cottage?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify the engineering change that cut coal use per unit of power
questions.stem: Early steam engines burned coal to boil water in a single cylinder, and much of the heat went into that cylinder rather than into motion. What change made steam power cheap enough to drive mills?

options.text: Condensing the steam in a second vessel beside the cylinder

options.misconception: mislabels a fuel change as the engine's key improvement
options.text: Burning wood instead of coal to make the running cost lower

options.misconception: confuses steam power with a water mill's natural site
options.text: Setting the boiler and cylinder in the stream below the mill

options.misconception: reverses the engine's operation into a cooling step
options.text: Pumping cold water into the cylinder after every stroke

questions.explanation: Condensing in a second vessel spared the power cylinder from being cooled and reheated on every stroke, so far less coal bought far more turning force. The tempting answer is a fuel substitution, when the gain came from the shape of the machine rather than from what it burned.
questions.hint: Where was the wasted heat going each stroke?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify how a fixed power source concentrated workers in one place
questions.stem: A mill beside a fast stream beat a mill two valleys away that had to pay to haul coal over bad roads. How did that single feature reshape where factory labor lived?

options.text: Owners gathered hands into one settlement beside the water

options.misconception: reverses the effect of a fixed power source on housing
options.text: Owners scattered hands widely to cut the cost of housing

options.misconception: makes damming a precondition for siting
options.text: Workers came only after the river had been dammed for mills

options.misconception: invents a ban on water wheels that never existed
options.text: Regulators banned water wheels so that mills used steam

questions.explanation: Falling water was the cheap power, and a wheel could not be moved once it was sunk, so the machine fixed the workplace and the wage packet near the stream. The tempting answer reverses the constraint, when a scarce power source concentrates people rather than spreading them out.
questions.hint: Can a water wheel be moved after it is installed?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how enclosure released rural workers for wage labor
questions.stem: Parliament enclosed common fields, and within a generation small farmers in two counties had sold their plots and taken wage work. What economic change did enclosure set in motion?

options.text: Landless labor seeking wages beside a shrinking village

options.misconception: invents cheap new plots for people who had lost them
options.text: Landless families buying new enclosed plots at low rates

options.misconception: confuses consolidation with the creation of a labor pool
options.text: Farmers raising output per acre on larger combined holdings

options.misconception: reverses who left the village and who remained
options.text: Wages rising because the village had fewer mouths to feed

questions.explanation: Enclosure converted a shared right to work into a wage sale, so the countryside began supplying the hands the mills needed while villages thinned out. The tempting answer credits enclosure with consolidation, which is a different effect of the same law rather than its effect on labor.
questions.hint: What did enclosure take away besides the hedges?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: synthesize the use of state power to shape industrial markets
questions.stem: A manufacturer persuades Parliament to close an import route his competitors used, the measure passes, and his exports grow for a decade. Which reading of that record is best supported?

options.text: State power was used to shape markets for home firms

options.misconception: overstates the measure into a total trade ban
options.text: The firm won because Parliament ended foreign competition

options.misconception: attributes growth to a material the record omits
options.text: The firm won because its goods needed no imported cotton

options.misconception: misreads a protectionist measure as free trade
options.text: The measure shows Parliament had adopted free trade policy

questions.explanation: The record shows an industrial interest using the state to reshape the market for its own benefit, which is why early industrialization reads as politically managed rather than purely spontaneous. The tempting answers are either a total claim or a date claim about policy, and the item supports neither.
questions.hint: Who asked the legislature to close that route, and who gained?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: evaluate competing single-cause explanations of industrial take-off
questions.stem: One explanation says Britain industrialized because its coal was cheap; another says because its wages were high. What does the occurrence of both facts actually show?

options.text: Cheap fuel and dear labor both rewarded capital over hands

options.misconception: makes high wages an obstacle to machine investment
options.text: Cheap coal mattered while high wages slowed every investment

options.misconception: treats coal price as the only measure of output
options.text: High wages mattered while coal price set the level of output

options.misconception: presumes two true facts must cancel each other
options.text: The two explanations cancel out and explain nothing at all

questions.explanation: Take-off happened where power was cheap and labor expensive, because that combination paid firms to spend on machines, so naming either factor alone as decisive drops half the incentive. The tempting answers make one of the two prices work against investment, which is the opposite of the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Add the two incentives together rather than choosing one.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Incomes and population in early industrial Britain
questions.learningObjective: read the sequence of income and population curves against each other
questions.stem: Two records sit side by side: output per head in an English county rises slowly from 1750 to 1780 and quickly from 1800 to 1830, while the county's population curve bends upward only after 1800. What does the sequence suggest?

options.text: Income rose first, then better food let numbers grow faster

options.misconception: reverses the sequence into population as the first cause
options.text: Population grew first and caused every rise in output per head

options.misconception: declares mutual cause without reading the timing
options.text: Both curves rose at once, so neither can explain the other

options.misconception: inverts the direction of output per head against numbers
options.text: Output per head fell as population rose, confirming each other

questions.explanation: The order matters: incomes had to improve before population accelerated, and the extra hands then supplied the labor the machines employed. The tempting answer reverses the sequence into a chicken-and-egg story, which the dates printed on the two curves contradict.
questions.hint: Which curve bends first, and what does the other do after?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify how steam power freed works from water sites
questions.stem: In the 1780s an ironmaster built pipes and bar in a coal valley where no fast stream ran nearby. What made production possible in that spot?

options.text: A steam engine that raised water whatever the local fall

options.misconception: confuses steam power with transport of iron by canal
options.text: A canal widened the river that carried fuel to the works

options.misconception: invents wind power at a valley-floor ironworks
options.text: Wind power from a tower on the ridge above the works

options.misconception: describes a gravity water supply, not mechanical power
options.text: A new aqueduct carried hill water down to the furnaces

questions.explanation: Once power came from burning fuel, the works no longer had to stand where water fell, so ironmasters moved into coal districts rather than river valleys. The tempting answers relocate the power in a transport channel or a gravity feed, which explains moving material rather than moving a pump.
questions.hint: What was the engine actually doing for the works?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: analyze the feedback between fuel demand and transport expansion
questions.stem: Steamships and railways both began by hauling coal, and their later route maps follow the seams almost exactly. What does that coincidence show about industrial growth?

options.text: Transport and fuel demand reinforced each other locally

options.misconception: substitutes a market conspiracy for a cost mechanism
options.text: Coal firms chose the routes secretly to raise their shares

options.misconception: reverses the sequence by ending the coal trade first
options.text: Railways were built only after the coal trade had ended

options.misconception: makes geology the sole determinant of every route
options.text: Coal seams alone fixed every railway route regardless of traffic

questions.explanation: Cheap coal lowered the running cost of engines and engines widened the market for coal, so power and transport grew as one self-reinforcing system in particular regions. The tempting answers are a conspiracy or a monopoly claim, and neither explains why the seams line up with the lines.
questions.hint: What did engines burn, and what did that do to demand?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how transport cost passed through to urban food prices
questions.stem: A town sixty miles inland saw bread prices fall within a year of the railway opening. Which mechanism best explains that fall?

options.text: Cheap carriage of grain opened distant markets to buyers

options.misconception: confuses grain transport cost with bakery wages
options.text: Railway wages fell so bakers could afford to charge less

options.misconception: invents a price cap tied to the railway opening
options.text: The government capped bread prices when the line opened

options.misconception: substitutes a crop shift for the transport change
options.text: Farmers stopped growing wheat and planted cheaper crops

questions.explanation: Before rail, grain spoiled before it could reach distant buyers, which kept local prices high, so the binding charge between harvest and table was transport rather than baking. The tempting answer is the one that comes from an economic model rather than from the physical limits of the commodity itself.
questions.hint: What did the miller pay before the line existed?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: trace the link between enslaved plantation labor and European manufacturing
questions.stem: A mill ledger records bales arriving from a plantation port across the Atlantic, and the same year's port records show shipping tonnage doubling. What best connects the two records?

options.text: Enslaved-grown fiber fed mills that grew European trade

options.misconception: reverses the direction into a shipbuilding loop
options.text: European shipwrights built the mills that built the ships

options.misconception: claims falling prices cut the number of spinners
options.text: Falling cotton prices let mills hire fewer spinners each year

options.misconception: attributes port growth to timber rather than crops
options.text: The port's tonnage grew from timber, not from any crop

questions.explanation: Enslaved labor grew the fiber, the fiber kept the mills supplied, and cheap cloth sustained the trade that built the shipping that carried more fiber, so the connection runs through forced labor in the field. The tempting answer is a tidy loop, but cotton does not build ships.
questions.hint: What grew the fiber that the mills consumed?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: analyze where the capital for early factories came from
questions.stem: A merchant's ledger shows profits from goods and slave trading reinvested in spinning frames, while the interest rate on such loans remained high. How did industry mainly get its capital?

options.text: Accumulated merchant profits ploweded back into mills

options.misconception: invents abundant cheap overseas credit for early mills
options.text: Fresh overseas coin, lent cheaply by continental banks

options.misconception: credits the state with low-cost industrial loans
options.text: Government loans to manufacturers at low fixed interest rates

options.misconception: confuses worker savings with the capital that built mills
options.text: Savings of new wage workers, gathered in friendly societies

questions.explanation: The scale of new fixed capital came from trading profits already inside the country, which is why the first industrialists were merchants and mill owners rather than bankers. The tempting answers are a money-supply story or a state-loan story, and the high lending rate in the item undercuts the cheap-credit version.
questions.hint: Whose profits were already in the country before the mills?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how limited exclusivity rewarded invention
questions.stem: A 1765 English act let an inventor exclude others from a new process for a limited term. Why did that matter for industrial growth?

options.text: Inventors could recover research costs before copying began

options.misconception: converts a limited term into a permanent monopoly
options.text: Inventors were promised a permanent monopoly on every machine

options.misconception: replaces patent rights with a state purchase guarantee
options.text: Parliament promised to buy every machine an inventor made

options.misconception: invents an export ban rather than an exclusive right
options.text: Foreign rivals were barred from visiting English workshops

questions.explanation: A time-limited exclusive right gives an inventor a few years to earn back development costs, which is exactly the gamble that drawing and spinning improvements required. The tempting answer confuses a limited term with the permanent monopoly that made some later patents politically controversial.
questions.hint: How long did the exclusive right last?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how fines and posted rules imposed time discipline
questions.stem: Mill rules fined a worker for arriving late, talking during weaving, or breaking a shuttle, and the fines were posted by the door. What problem was that machinery of rules built to solve?

options.text: Making machine-paced work predictable by policing time

options.misconception: reads discipline rules as an attempt to raise skill
options.text: Raising the skill level of the handloom weavers it used

options.misconception: confuses shop-floor fines with statutory wage fixing
options.text: Fixing wages by law so that every worker earned the same sum

options.misconception: reverses who held authority over the shop floor
options.text: Handing control of the shop floor to elected committees

questions.explanation: A powered line only pays if every worker keeps time, so fines and posted rules converted a seasonal craft habit into a rhythm a supervisor could audit from a list. The tempting answer sounds like worker power, whereas these rules concentrated control in the owner's bookkeeper.
questions.hint: What breaks first when a machine sets the pace?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: design a response to machine-breaking that addresses the underlying grievance
questions.stem: Machine-breaking spreads among weavers whose rates the new frames have cut, and crowds now call the frames themselves the enemy. Which response would most reduce the violence?

options.text: Set a public wage floor and back new machinery research

options.misconception: treats a wages grievance as a disorder for troops
options.text: Send troops to smash the machines and jail every breaker

options.misconception: offers a promise the owners were never going to keep
options.text: Promise the frames will vanish, then quietly keep using them

options.misconception: concedes the machine-burners the destruction they wanted
options.text: Permit the crowds to break frames and pay to replace them

questions.explanation: The crowd's real claim was about rates, so a wage floor plus public money for better machinery answers the interest behind the violence and takes the frame out of private hands that profit from it. The tempting answer is suppression, which treats a wages grievance as though it were a riot to be policed.
questions.hint: What were the breakers actually angry about?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: analyze why industrial workers' demands frightened rulers
questions.stem: A reform meeting in a northern industrial city in 1819 was met by cavalry that cut through the crowd. What made the demand there so hard for rulers to concede?

options.text: Newly enfranchised wage earners asked for political power itself

options.misconception: casts demonstrators as mutinous soldiers rather than voters
options.text: The demonstrators were soldiers refusing to drill for magistrates

options.misconception: invites the crown to have called the reform meeting
options.text: The crown had called the meeting to test a new militia

options.misconception: substitutes a factory inspection grievance for a vote
options.text: The crowd demanded the abolition of factory inspection

questions.explanation: A crowd of newly qualified voters organizing as a class asked for the ballot, and that made the demand about power rather than a wage the crown could concede, which is why troops met it. The tempting answer puts the initiative with the crown, when the meeting had assembled itself without orders.
questions.hint: What were they asking for, rather than complaining about?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why the 1832 settlement disappointed organized workers
questions.stem: After a decade of pressure, Parliament in 1832 gave the vote to middle-class householders and moved ten Irish seats elsewhere. Why did the crowds go home disappointed?

options.text: Working men still had no vote and the seats were reallocated

options.misconception: claims a voting reform replaced the monarchy outright
options.text: The reform had abolished the monarchy and made a republic

options.misconception: overstates the reform as universal male suffrage
options.text: The reform had given the vote to every adult man at once

options.misconception: reverses the act's central work of redistributing seats
options.text: The reform had restored all the old rotten borough practices

questions.explanation: A settlement that widened the electorate only for taxpaying householders left the organized workers of the new towns without a vote, so the law solved the middle class's problem while preserving the system's shape. The tempting answer mistakes a reform for a democratization.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain paternal reform as a management proposal rather than socialism
questions.stem: A Scottish mill owner shortened the working day, raised children's minimum wages, and built a school and a hall, while still owning the mill and taking the profits. What was he trying to show?

options.text: Better conditions would make workers steady partners in the firm

options.misconception: frames the scheme as a plan to destroy rival mills
options.text: Better conditions would bankrupt the older mills in England

options.misconception: mistakes paternalism for giving the mill to workers
options.text: Workers would come to own the mill outright by his gift

options.misconception: turns a management experiment into a claim about voting
options.text: Winning the vote would make owners redundant in the works

questions.explanation: Owen argued that profit and morale were compatible, since shorter hours and schooling would produce steadier workers, so his philanthropy was a management proposal rather than an abolition of ownership. The tempting answer is the one that sounds like socialism, and worker ownership was precisely what he was not offering.
questions.hint: Who kept the profits at the end of his experiment?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why class vocabulary helped workers organize
questions.stem: From 1821 organizers in a mill town signed wage earners up in friendly societies and named employers a class apart from workers. Why was that vocabulary useful?

options.text: It turned scattered grievances into an interest to organize

options.misconception: mistakes class vocabulary for a legal estate system
options.text: It recorded the kingdom's own division into legal orders

options.misconception: assumes the new societies revived the old guilds
options.text: It revived the craft guilds that had run the town's trade

options.misconception: confuses collective bargaining with industrial voting
options.text: It let the new voters choose their own mill managers

questions.explanation: Naming the other side as a class gave scattered wage earners a shared opponent and a reason to keep meeting, which is what made sustained strikes possible where earlier riots had failed. questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: analyze how piece rates transferred gains to the mill owner
questions.stem: A weaver's real pay falls even as his output per hour rises, because the price the mill pays for a length of cloth drops faster still. What has the payment system done to his craft?

options.text: Bought his work in pieces, so faster hands earn less

options.misconception: assumes rising output raised the hourly rate too
options.text: Given him more training so that his hourly rate rose with output

options.misconception: replaces a payment change with a machine no one can learn
options.text: Replaced his skill with a machine no worker could learn to use

options.misconception: confuses a rate-setting practice with wage legislation
options.text: Fixed his wage by law so the cloth price could not fall

questions.explanation: Under piece rates the owner gains from every cut in the price of the piece, so a faster weaver's rising output is exactly what gets him paid less in real terms, and that is how a skilled craft became interchangeable. questions.learningObjective: explain why the 1833 act cost owners little to obey
questions.stem: The 1833 act barred children under twelve from textile mills and set a maximum day of eleven hours. Why did many owners obey without waiting for an inspector?

options.text: Machinery made long shifts unsafe, so the law matched the trade

options.misconception: reverses the fine into a reason to hide the violation
options.text: The fine for breaking the rule exceeded the labor it saved

options.misconception: invents a state subsidy for ending child labor

questions.learningObjective: analyze why well-evidenced reports produced no reform
questions.stem: Read the record: a parliamentary commission in 1844 named specific yards, wages, and hours, and its report was printed and sold widely. Why did little change for a decade?

questions.learningObjective: analyze how optional legislation left the neediest towns unprotected
questions.stem: After a cholera outbreak, Parliament in 1848 allowed towns to raise a small rate for sewers but left the choice to them. What weakness followed from that design?

options.text: The neediest cities could still decline to pay for sewers

options.text: The rate was set so high that no town could ever afford it

options.misconception: reverses the sequence of vote and construction

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Rebuilding a capital under a military government
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the motives behind wholesale urban demolition
questions.stem: A prefect with a shallow treasury, a large army, and a city whose narrow streets block movement proposes to demolish whole districts and rebuild them with sewers and boulevards. Which motive best explains the timing?

options.text: The same trenches gave sewers and troop movement

options.misconception: reduces the rebuild to a single technical necessity
options.text: No other way existed to widen streets in the old quarter

options.misconception: overstates repair failure into proof of impossibility
options.text: Engineers had proved that partial repairs could never work

options.misconception: invents a council vote the record omits
options.text: The council had already voted funds for a sewer network

questions.explanation: The scheme answered three problems at once, because trenches for sewers and straight roads for troops came with the same demolition, and the cleared ground also made the quarter easier to police and to cannon across. The tempting answer credits engineering necessity alone, which leaves the political motive unexplained.
questions.hint: What did the wide new streets do besides carry sewage?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: synthesize why latecomers built steel and chemicals instead of cloth
questions.stem: Germany and the United States built steel, chemical, and electrical industries after 1870 without ever passing through a mature cloth trade. What best explains that difference?

options.text: Newest processes let them enter at the leading edge

options.misconception: invents a merchant boycott of textile machinery
options.text: Their merchants refused to invest in textile machinery at all

options.misconception: attributes the shift to a rural protectionist law
options.text: Their governments banned cloth mills to protect farms

options.misconception: explains investment by a wage demand in one trade
options.text: Their workers demanded higher wages for textile work alone

questions.explanation: Where the earlier wave mechanized a spinning and weaving that already existed, a later entrant could buy the newest steel, chemical, and electrical processes whole and never build a cloth mill, so the second wave favored new states. The tempting answers build the difference out of clerk or worker preference, which the record does not show.
questions.hint: What could a latecomer buy that a pioneer had to invent?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish science-based industry from mechanized craft production
questions.stem: A chapter lists the fastest-growing industries after 1870 as steel, chemicals, electrical goods, and refined oil. What distinguishes that list from the earlier industrial wave?

options.text: They rested on science and heavy capital rather than on cloth

options.misconception: describes the cottage trades these industries replaced
options.text: They were small craft trades run out of family workshops

options.misconception: confuses steam and electricity with hand power
options.text: They depended on hand power in scattered rural cottages

options.misconception: invents a railway collapse that never occurred
options.text: They grew only after every railway in Europe closed

questions.explanation: The earlier wave mechanized a spinning and weaving that already existed, while the later one built entirely new processes out of laboratory chemistry and heavy fixed capital, so the new sectors drew on science and investment rather than an inherited craft. The tempting answer is the workshop version, which describes the industry these processes displaced.
questions.hint: Where did the new processes come from, and how much capital did they need?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the strongest argument for a colonial tariff
questions.stem: A minister in 1905 defends a colonial tariff that keeps foreign cloth out of his colony. Which judgment best weighs the strongest argument in its favor?

options.text: A protected buyer lets a young mill reach scale and hire

options.misconception: invents an empty colonial export economy that never existed
options.text: The colony produced nothing worth sending to the mother country

options.misconception: makes imported cloth cheaper and better, defeating the policy
options.text: Imported cloth there was always cheaper and always better made

options.misconception: credits a fiscal motive with no fiscal evidence
options.text: The tariff filled the treasury at no political cost at all

questions.explanation: The strongest case is developmental rather than fiscal: a tariff lets a young industry reach scale before it meets world prices, at the cost of charging colonial buyers more, which is a real trade-off rather than a free gain. The tempting answer takes the cheapest-goods claim, which cuts against the policy's whole purpose.
questions.hint: Who pays the higher price, and what does the mill gain?
